findings.summary: The subject correctly establishes that an odd-cardinality no-three-in-line set invariant under a half-turn has at most one point; hence a 153-point set cannot have half-turn symmetry about any center.
The subject correctly establishes that a quarter-turn-invariant no-three-in-line set has cardinality divisible by four or equal to one, excluding cardinalities 153 and 154.
The subject correctly shows that a half-turn-invariant 154-point subset of the 77-by-77 grid must be centered at (38,38), with the center unoccupied.

The centered-half-turn conclusion is repairable, but the written argument omits a classification excluding other finite-order lattice rotations about arbitrary centers. Moreover, rct4 is only a strict subclass of centered half-turn configurations, not the entire remaining rotational route.

Static inspection supports that the n=77 model exactly encodes the stated 154-point rct4 subclass: its orbit counts, primitive-line enumeration, weighted line constraints, CNF translation, and deterministic statistics are sound and complete within that subclass.

The five committed certificates at n=41, 47, 57, 65, and 69 provide exact implementation regression checks at those sizes only; they do not establish the broader historical range claim, provenance, or discovery priority.

The reported UNKNOWN results and timeouts prove neither satisfiability nor unsatisfiability of the n=77 rct4 instance. The absence of committed logs or proof traces and comparable failures on known satisfiable calibration sizes give the timeouts no negative mathematical force.

The subject supplies neither a 153- or 154-point certificate nor a global upper-bound improvement, so D(77) remains unresolved with the certified interval 152 ≤ D(77) ≤ 154; even rct4 infeasibility would exclude only that restricted subclass.
